title: A Survey on Computer-Aided Diagnosis for Ocular Diseases

subsections.section_title: Clinical Scope and Disease Taxonomy in Computer-Aided Ocular Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Major ocular diseases and diagnostic priorities
subsections.content:
Computer-aided ocular diagnosis has concentrated on diseases that are prevalent, vision-threatening, and amenable to image-based screening. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains the dominant target because of its global burden and the feasibility of detecting referable disease from color fundus photographs at scale; major validation studies have shown that deep learning systems can achieve clinically useful sensitivity and specificity for DR detection and grading ref [1], ref [2]. Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is another priority because progression to late neovascular or atrophic stages causes irreversible central vision loss, motivating automated identification of drusen, pigmentary abnormalities, and late AMD markers in both fundus and OCT imaging ref [3], ref [4].

Glaucoma is diagnostically important but computationally more challenging because structural damage evolves gradually and labels are often noisy or definition-dependent. CAD systems therefore commonly focus on optic nerve head cupping, retinal nerve fiber layer loss, and multimodal risk estimation from fundus photographs and OCT ref [5], ref [6]. Retinal vascular disorders such as retinopathy of prematurity and retinal vein occlusion also attract attention where early triage can alter outcomes; in particular, plus disease assessment in retinopathy of prematurity has become a prominent benchmark for image-based severity analysis ref [7].

Beyond posterior-segment disease, cataract and corneal disorders are important because they are highly prevalent and relevant to community screening and teleophthalmology. Population-based AI studies have demonstrated automated identification of visually significant cataract and other referable ophthalmic abnormalities from slit-lamp and fundus data ref [8], ref [9]. Across these disease groups, diagnostic priorities are typically framed around screening for referable disease, grading severity, predicting progression, and supporting triage in settings where specialist access is limited ref [1], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Scope and Disease Taxonomy in Computer-Aided Ocular Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Anatomical structures and pathological biomarkers
subsections.content:
Computer-aided ocular diagnosis is grounded in the anatomy that imaging modalities make visible: the optic nerve head, retinal nerve fiber layer, macula, retinal vasculature, choroid, and anterior segment structures. In fundus photography and OCT, these structures provide the substrate for disease-specific biomarkers, such as cup-to-disc configuration for glaucoma, vessel caliber and branching abnormalities for hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy, and macular thickness or outer retinal disruption for macular disease. The clinical centrality of these markers is reflected in standardized studies of optic disc damage, diabetic retinopathy severity, and age-related macular degeneration grading systems ref [11], ref [12], ref [13].

Pathological biomarkers span both morphologic lesions and quantitative tissue measurements. For diabetic retinopathy, microaneurysms, hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, and neovascularization remain the canonical lesion set used by automated systems ref [12], ref [14]. In glaucoma, structural injury is expressed by neuroretinal rim loss, enlarged cup-to-disc ratio, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thinning, and characteristic visual-field-correlated optic nerve head changes ref [11], ref [15]. For age-related macular degeneration, drusen burden, pigmentary abnormalities, geographic atrophy, and choroidal neovascular features define risk and stage, while OCT-derived biomarkers such as subretinal fluid, intraretinal fluid, and pigment epithelial detachment are especially important in neovascular disease ref [13], ref [16].

OCT has also expanded biomarker modeling from visible lesions to layered microstructure. Consensus nomenclature for retinal and choroidal anatomy has enabled reproducible segmentation of intraretinal layers and fluid compartments, supporting CAD systems for edema, tractional disorders, and inherited or neurodegenerative retinal disease ref [17]. In retinopathy of prematurity, vessel tortuosity and dilation quantified from posterior pole images operationalize plus disease ref [18]. More broadly, the success of image-based deep learning in ophthalmology depends on whether models can reliably capture these clinically meaningful anatomic targets rather than only global image appearance ref [10].

For survey purposes, anatomical structures are therefore not merely image regions of interest; they are the carriers of biomarkers that connect automated measurements to ophthalmic reasoning. A useful taxonomy distinguishes stable anatomy to be segmented, local lesions to be detected, diffuse tissue alterations to be quantified, and longitudinal biomarkers to be monitored across visits.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Scope and Disease Taxonomy in Computer-Aided Ocular Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic tasks in ophthalmic CAD
subsections.content:
Diagnostic tasks in ophthalmic computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) span a continuum from image-level screening to lesion-level characterization and longitudinal risk assessment. At the broadest level, systems perform binary or multi-class disease detection from fundus photographs or OCT volumes, as exemplified by automated diabetic retinopathy screening and referral recommendation pipelines in retinal photography and OCT-based referral triage for macular disease and glaucoma-related damage ref [1], ref [10], ref [19]. These tasks are clinically motivated by the need to separate normal, non-urgent, and referable cases under population-scale screening constraints.

A second group of tasks targets anatomical and pathological quantification. Here, CAD systems localize the optic disc and cup, segment retinal layers and fluid compartments, and detect specific lesions such as microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, drusen, or geographic atrophy regions ref [20], ref [21], ref [22], ref [23]. Such outputs support disease grading, biomarker extraction, and explainable decision support, since clinically meaningful intermediate measurements—cup-to-disc ratio, central retinal thickness, drusen burden, or intraretinal/subretinal fluid extent—often align more closely with ophthalmic workflows than end-to-end labels alone.

Increasingly, ophthalmic CAD also addresses prognostic and workflow-oriented tasks, including disease progression prediction, treatment response estimation, image quality assessment, and multi-disease triage across heterogeneous imaging devices ref [24], ref [25], ref [26]. These tasks reflect the maturation of the field from isolated classification benchmarks toward clinically integrated systems that prioritize robustness, temporal modeling, and actionable outputs for screening programs, specialist referral, and follow-up management.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Scope and Disease Taxonomy in Computer-Aided Ocular Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical workflows and use scenarios
subsections.content:
Clinical deployment of ophthalmic CAD is shaped by where images are acquired and how decisions are escalated. In population screening, automated systems are typically used as front-end triage tools to identify referable disease from color fundus photographs or OCT, reducing specialist burden while preserving sensitivity for vision-threatening pathology. This workflow has been most clearly articulated for diabetic retinopathy screening, where autonomous or semi-autonomous AI can support point-of-care referral decisions in primary care or endocrinology settings rather than ophthalmology clinics ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. Similar screening-oriented use cases have been explored for glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration, although these tasks often require multimodal evidence and longitudinal confirmation ref [30], ref [1].

Within specialty clinics, CAD more often functions as a decision-support layer embedded in image review, prioritization, and documentation rather than as a fully autonomous diagnostic endpoint. Deep learning systems have shown utility for referral refinement, lesion quantification, and risk stratification from retinal photographs and OCT, with potential roles in virtual clinics and teleophthalmology pathways ref [10], ref [22]. Workflow integration is especially relevant in emergency and underserved settings, where image-based triage can expand access to expert interpretation and reduce delays in management ref [31].

A clinically meaningful use scenario therefore depends not only on algorithmic accuracy but also on image quality control, interoperability with acquisition devices, predefined referral thresholds, and prospective validation in the intended care pathway. Studies emphasizing externally validated and real-world evaluation highlight that safe adoption requires matching model outputs to concrete actions such as rescreening, specialist referral, or treatment monitoring ref [28], ref [29], ref [32], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Ophthalmic Imaging Modalities and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Color fundus photography
subsections.content:
Color fundus photography (CFP) is the most widely deployed retinal imaging modality in computer-aided ophthalmic diagnosis because it is inexpensive, noninvasive, and compatible with large-scale screening workflows. Standard CFP provides two-dimensional en face visualization of the optic disc, macula, retinal vessels, and posterior pole lesions, enabling assessment of diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma-related disc change, hypertensive retinopathy, and vascular occlusions. The modality’s public health importance is reflected in landmark teleophthalmology and automated screening studies for diabetic retinopathy, which demonstrated that CFP can support both human grading and algorithmic triage at scale ref [34], ref [1].

From an image analysis perspective, CFP supports a broad spectrum of tasks, including vessel segmentation, optic disc and cup localization, lesion detection, image quality assessment, and disease grading. Canonical benchmarks such as DRIVE and STARE established reproducible evaluation for retinal vessel analysis ref [35], ref [36], while Messidor and EyePACS enabled development of referral-grade diabetic retinopathy systems and modern deep learning pipelines ref [37], ref [38], ref [39]. More recently, large multitask studies have shown that CFP can be used not only for ocular diagnosis but also for systemic risk prediction, underscoring the richness of retinal phenotypes captured in routine photographs ref [40].

Nevertheless, CFP has important limitations that shape dataset design and annotation protocols. Image appearance varies substantially with camera type, field of view, mydriatic status, compression, pigmentation, and illumination, and two-dimensional projections cannot resolve cross-sectional retinal microstructure available in OCT. Ungradable images remain a major source of deployment error, motivating explicit quality labels and standardized grading schemes. Clinical standards from the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study and the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy severity scale continue to influence annotation granularity, field definition, and outcome labeling in contemporary CFP datasets ref [41], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Ophthalmic Imaging Modalities and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Optical coherence tomography and OCT angiography
subsections.content:
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the principal cross-sectional imaging modality in retinal diagnostics, providing micrometer-scale visualization of retinal and choroidal layers and enabling quantitative biomarkers such as retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, central macular thickness, drusen burden, and intraretinal or subretinal fluid. The transition from time-domain to spectral-domain and swept-source OCT improved acquisition speed, axial resolution, and penetration, making dense volumetric analysis feasible in glaucoma, diabetic macular edema, and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) ref [1], ref [2]. For computer-aided diagnosis, OCT data pose modality-specific challenges: 3D volumes are anisotropic, device-dependent, and often affected by speckle noise, motion, and segmentation failure, so algorithm design often relies on layer-aware preprocessing and volume-based learning rather than single B-scan classification ref [3], ref [4].

OCT angiography (OCTA) extends OCT by detecting motion contrast from erythrocytes to visualize retinal and choroidal microvasculature without dye injection. Compared with fluorescein angiography, OCTA better resolves depth-stratified vascular plexuses and neovascular membranes, but it is more sensitive to projection artifacts, attenuation beneath drusen or hemorrhage, and limited field of view ref [5], ref [6]. Clinically relevant OCTA endpoints for automated analysis include vessel density, foveal avascular zone morphology, nonperfusion, and choriocapillaris flow deficits, which have shown value in diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD assessment ref [7], ref [8].

From a data-resource perspective, OCT and OCTA require richer annotations than color fundus photographs. Labels may be assigned at eye, volume, B-scan, pixel, or layer level, and robust curation often combines expert grading with manual correction of device-generated segmentations, standardized scan protocols, and quality control for signal strength and motion artifacts. Public datasets such as Duke OCT and retinal fluid benchmarks have accelerated segmentation and diagnostic modeling, but cross-device generalization remains a major limitation because acquisition protocols and voxel geometry differ substantially across vendors ref [9], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Ophthalmic Imaging Modalities and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Slit-lamp, anterior segment, and corneal imaging
subsections.content:
Slit-lamp and other anterior-segment imaging modalities provide complementary views of the cornea, conjunctiva, iris, lens, and periocular structures, and are therefore central to computer-aided assessment of cataract, keratitis, pterygium, keratoconus, and dry-eye-related surface disease. In contrast to posterior-segment fundus imaging, these data are strongly affected by illumination geometry, specular reflection, magnification, and acquisition protocol, which makes cross-device generalization especially difficult. Early automated cataract grading from slit-lamp photographs demonstrated the feasibility of image-based severity estimation using lens opacity patterns and texture cues, while subsequent work showed that deep convolutional models can support referral decisions from routine slit-lamp images ref [42], ref [43].

For corneal disease, imaging spans broad-view slit-lamp photography and high-resolution modalities such as in vivo confocal microscopy and corneal topography/tomography. Deep learning has achieved expert-level or near-expert screening performance for infectious keratitis from external eye or slit-lamp photographs, supporting triage where corneal specialists are scarce ref [44], ref [45]. In parallel, AI on in vivo confocal microscopy has been used for detecting fungal elements and acanthamoeba cysts, illustrating how modality choice determines the scale of visible pathology and annotation granularity ref [46], ref [47]. Keratoconus detection has similarly benefited from quantitative anterior-segment maps, where machine learning on Scheimpflug-derived parameters can identify subclinical ectasia beyond subjective interpretation ref [48].

From a data perspective, anterior-segment datasets require carefully standardized labels because clinically meaningful targets range from image-level diagnosis to lesion localization and severity staging. Large-scale curation efforts for cataract and pediatric ocular disease have highlighted the value of multi-center image acquisition, explicit quality control, and clinically grounded grading schemes for building deployable models ref [49], ref [50]. More recent work on slit-lamp-based deep learning systems further emphasizes the need to document staining protocol, illumination condition, and device metadata, since these factors materially affect reproducibility and domain shift ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Ophthalmic Imaging Modalities and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Fluorescein angiography, ultrasound, and multimodal imaging
subsections.content:
Fluorescein angiography (FA) remains important when dynamic vascular information is required, because it directly depicts dye transit, leakage, staining, capillary nonperfusion, and neovascularization that are not fully represented in static color fundus images. In diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusion, ultra-widefield FA has been particularly valuable for quantifying peripheral ischemia and relating ischemic burden to macular edema or neovascular complications, while also revealing lesion distributions missed by conventional posterior-pole imaging ref [52], ref [53]. More recently, deep learning has been explored for automatic interpretation of FA sequences and leakage patterns, including phase-wise diabetic retinopathy grading and lesion analysis, indicating that temporal angiographic information can support severity assessment beyond single-frame appearance ref [54].

Ophthalmic ultrasound, especially B-scan imaging, is complementary when optical media are opaque or when posterior segment structures cannot be visualized directly. It is routinely used for vitreoretinal disorders, retinal detachment, choroidal tumors, and traumatic pathology, and standardized echography remains a core reference framework for ocular and orbital diagnosis ref [55], ref [56]. From a computer-aided diagnosis perspective, ultrasound poses distinctive challenges: low signal-to-noise ratio, speckle, operator dependence, and comparatively limited public datasets. Consequently, most computational work has focused on narrower tasks such as tumor characterization or segmentation rather than large-scale foundation-model-style screening pipelines.

Multimodal imaging integrates structural, vascular, and clinical context across modalities such as color fundus photography, OCT/OCTA, FA, and ultrasound. Cross-modal learning is attractive because different modalities expose complementary disease mechanisms: FA highlights leakage and perfusion dynamics, OCT captures retinal microstructure, and fundus photographs preserve global lesion appearance. Recent machine learning studies show that multimodal fusion can improve diagnosis, prognosis, and referral decisions in retinal disease compared with single-modality systems ref [57], ref [24], ref [10]. Large clinically curated multimodal resources are therefore increasingly important, exemplified by ophthalmic datasets linking images with longitudinal labels and treatment outcomes, although harmonizing acquisition protocols, temporal alignment, and annotation schemas remains a major bottleneck ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Ophthalmic Imaging Modalities and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Public datasets, annotation protocols, and data curation
subsections.content:
Public ophthalmic datasets have been central to benchmarking automated diagnosis, but they vary markedly in modality, label granularity, and acquisition bias. In color fundus imaging, widely used resources such as DRIVE, STARE, MESSIDOR, EyePACS/Kaggle diabetic retinopathy collections, and ODIR differ in camera models, field of view, disease prevalence, and whether annotations target pixels, lesions, or patient-level grades, which complicates direct comparison across studies [1,2,3,4,5]. Similar issues arise in OCT and multimodal datasets, where device-specific appearance and scan protocols strongly affect downstream model generalization [6].

Annotation protocols are equally important because ophthalmic labels often require expert adjudication and standardized grading rules. For diabetic retinopathy, the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy and Diabetic Macular Edema Disease Severity Scales provided a common framework later operationalized at scale in deep learning studies using multiple graders and arbitration [7,8]. For glaucoma and optic nerve assessment, the subjectivity of cup-to-disc boundary definition has motivated contour-based benchmarks such as RIGA and explicit documentation of inter-observer variability [9]. In OCT, clinically meaningful labels may combine retinal layer boundaries, fluid compartments, and disease categories, requiring hierarchical annotation workflows [6].

Data curation therefore extends beyond de-identification and train-test splitting. Best practice includes image quality control, exclusion criteria for media opacity or severe artifacts, provenance tracking across devices and sites, and external validation on geographically distinct cohorts to reduce hidden stratification [5,8,10]. Recent work also emphasizes preserving uncertainty through consensus or probabilistic labels rather than forcing a single deterministic ground truth, especially for borderline disease and poor-quality images [8,9].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations of Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Image preprocessing and enhancement
subsections.content:
Image preprocessing is a prerequisite for reliable ocular CAD because fundus photography, OCT, and slit-lamp images exhibit large variability in illumination, contrast, field of view, and device-specific artifacts. Early retinal pipelines therefore standardized color and local contrast before downstream analysis, often using channel selection, background estimation, and normalization to improve vessel and lesion visibility. Classical reviews of retinal image analysis emphasized the importance of denoising, shade correction, and contrast enhancement as foundational steps for robust detection of vasculature, optic disc, and pathological signs such as microaneurysms and exudates ref [64], ref [65].

In fundus imaging, enhancement has often been tightly linked to vessel-aware processing. Matched filtering and related multiscale operators were introduced to amplify elongated vascular structures against uneven retinal background ref [66], while contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization became a common generic enhancement method because it improves local contrast without the excessive noise amplification associated with global histogram equalization ref [67]. For lesion-oriented screening, preprocessing can also include green-channel extraction, masking of nonretinal background, and illumination equalization prior to candidate generation; such steps were integral to classical diabetic retinopathy systems for exudate and red-lesion detection ref [68], ref [69].

In OCT and other cross-sectional modalities, the main objective is often speckle suppression and boundary preservation rather than color normalization. Comparative studies have shown that anisotropic diffusion and related edge-preserving filters improve the delineation of retinal layers while reducing speckle noise ref [70], and wavelet-based denoising has similarly been used to enhance pathological structures in OCT scans ref [71]. More recent learning-based CAD systems still retain preprocessing, but increasingly as light-touch standardization—resizing, intensity scaling, quality assessment, and artifact removal—because deep networks can learn part of the enhancement implicitly when trained on large heterogeneous datasets ref [1], ref [10].

Overall, preprocessing and enhancement should be viewed not as a fixed front end but as a modality- and task-dependent design choice that balances artifact suppression against preservation of subtle clinical cues. Excessive enhancement may alter lesion appearance or introduce domain shift, whereas insufficient normalization can degrade generalization across cameras, institutions, and populations.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations of Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Segmentation of anatomical structures and lesions
subsections.content:
Segmentation is a core intermediate task in ocular computer-aided diagnosis because many clinically meaningful biomarkers are spatially localized. In retinal fundus and OCT analysis, delineation of the optic disc/cup, blood vessels, retinal layers, and pathological regions enables explicit measurement of cup-to-disc ratio, vessel caliber and tortuosity, layer thickness, and lesion burden. Classical approaches relied on deformable models and graph-based optimization, exemplified by level-set optic disc/cup segmentation and graph-theoretic retinal layer segmentation in OCT, which offered anatomically constrained boundaries but were sensitive to image quality and hand-crafted priors [1,2].

For vascular and lesion analysis, supervised pixel-wise learning and structured prediction improved robustness over purely rule-based methods. Early benchmark studies on vessel extraction using line operators and matched filtering established the importance of multiscale representations [3], while later discriminative methods such as conditional random fields and random forests were used for exudate and microaneurysm region delineation [4]. Public challenges and datasets, including DRIVE for vessels and DIARETDB1 for diabetic retinopathy lesions, helped standardize evaluation and accelerated comparison across methods [5,6].

Deep convolutional segmentation networks now dominate ocular CAD. U-Net provided the template for data-efficient biomedical segmentation [7], and fully convolutional architectures were rapidly adapted to retinal vessels, optic disc/cup, and OCT fluids or layers [8,9]. More recently, nested skip connections and attention mechanisms have improved boundary preservation and small-lesion sensitivity in highly imbalanced settings [10]. Despite these advances, segmentation performance remains limited by domain shift across cameras and scanners, ambiguous lesion borders, and imperfect annotations, motivating weakly supervised, multitask, and uncertainty-aware formulations.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations of Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Handcrafted features and conventional machine learning
subsections.content:
Before deep learning became dominant, ocular computer-aided diagnosis relied on explicit feature engineering coupled with conventional classifiers. In retinal imaging, pipelines typically segmented vessels, optic disc, cup, exudates, microaneurysms, or hemorrhages, and then summarized lesion burden, vascular tortuosity, caliber, texture, and color statistics for disease grading. Early diabetic retinopathy systems used candidate lesion detection followed by handcrafted descriptors and rule-based or statistical classification, demonstrating that interpretable image cues could support large-scale screening ref [68], ref [81]. Similar strategies underpinned optic nerve head analysis for glaucoma, where cup-to-disc geometry, neuroretinal rim measures, and vessel-related features were linked to visual field loss and diagnosis ref [82], ref [83].

A major methodological theme was the use of generic texture and local appearance descriptors, including wavelets, Gabor filters, gray-level co-occurrence measures, local binary patterns, and histogram features, which were subsequently classified by k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, random forests, AdaBoost, or shallow neural networks. Texture-based approaches were especially influential for age-related macular degeneration and retinal lesion discrimination, while bag-of-features formulations offered robustness to local appearance variation ref [84], ref [85]. For diabetic retinopathy, ensemble-based lesion detectors and image-level classifiers showed that carefully designed handcrafted representations could achieve clinically useful sensitivity even without end-to-end learning ref [86], ref [87].

These methods offered important advantages: small-data suitability, lower computational cost, and partial clinical interpretability through direct correspondence between features and known biomarkers. However, their performance was constrained by task-specific preprocessing, limited invariance to imaging conditions, and the need for substantial expert design. Comparative studies in glaucoma and retinal disease later showed that learned representations increasingly surpassed manually crafted features, but conventional pipelines established many of the anatomical priors and evaluation protocols that modern ocular CAD still inherits ref [83], ref [88], ref [89].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations of Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Deep learning architectures for ocular diagnosis
subsections.content:
Deep learning has become the dominant paradigm in ocular computer-aided diagnosis because convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can learn hierarchical representations directly from fundus photographs, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and slit-lamp images. Early ophthalmic systems largely adapted classification backbones such as Inception and ResNet, demonstrating specialist-level diabetic retinopathy screening from color fundus photographs and establishing end-to-end image-to-diagnosis pipelines ref [1], ref [27]. Similar CNN frameworks were subsequently extended to glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration, where transfer learning and large-scale pretraining improved robustness under limited annotated data ref [5], ref [3].

For volumetric and cross-sectional OCT, architectural design has emphasized contextual aggregation across B-scans and retinal layers. CNNs trained on OCT volumes enabled automated referral recommendations for retinal disease, while hybrid systems combining attention mechanisms or recurrent components captured inter-slice dependencies and improved lesion-sensitive interpretation ref [10], ref [90]. In parallel, segmentation-oriented encoder-decoder models such as U-Net became central for delineating optic disc/cup, retinal layers, and fluid regions, often serving as a precursor or auxiliary branch for downstream diagnosis ref [77].

More recent work has moved beyond pure CNNs toward architectures that better model long-range structure and multimodal reasoning. Vision transformers and CNN-transformer hybrids have shown competitive performance on retinal image analysis benchmarks, especially when pretrained at scale or adapted through self-supervision ref [91]. In clinically deployed settings, however, architectural choice is increasingly evaluated not only by accuracy but also by calibration, interpretability, and external validity; studies on deep learning for retinal disease detection have highlighted the need for saliency assessment, uncertainty estimation, and cross-device generalization before routine adoption ref [32], ref [92].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations of Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal, weakly supervised, and self-supervised learning
subsections.content:
Recent ocular CAD systems increasingly move beyond single-image supervised learning toward multimodal fusion, where color fundus photographs, OCT/OCTA, visual fields, and clinical metadata are jointly modeled to improve robustness and clinical relevance. In ophthalmology, deep learning has shown that structural and functional modalities can be linked to support diagnosis and prognosis, as illustrated by the prediction of OCT-derived retinal nerve fiber layer thickness from fundus images for glaucoma assessment and by multimodal imaging studies for age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy ref [93], ref [94], ref [3]. More broadly, multimodal retinal representation learning has been enabled by paired image-text resources, with RETFound demonstrating scalable foundation models across heterogeneous ophthalmic images and tasks ref [95].

Weakly supervised learning is particularly attractive in ocular imaging because dense lesion or layer annotations are expensive and often unavailable, whereas image-level labels from screening workflows are abundant. Multiple-instance and attention-based formulations have therefore been adopted to localize diabetic retinopathy lesions or glaucoma-relevant regions using only eye- or image-level supervision, reducing annotation burden while retaining interpretability ref [96], ref [97]. Related work on clinically applicable referable diabetic retinopathy systems also highlights the importance of uncertainty estimation and label quality when supervision is noisy or incomplete ref [1].

Self-supervised learning further addresses data scarcity by exploiting unlabeled ophthalmic images through contrastive, masked, or cross-modal pretraining. General frameworks such as Momentum Contrast, SimCLR, and masked autoencoders have been adapted to medical and retinal imaging to learn transferable representations from large uncurated archives ref [98], ref [99], ref [100]. In practice, these strategies are most useful when combined with multimodal alignment and weak labels, yielding encoders that can be fine-tuned for downstream grading, segmentation, and risk prediction with substantially fewer expert annotations.

subsections.section_title: Disease-Specific Computer-Aided Diagnostic Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema
subsections.content:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has been the most extensively studied ocular application of computer-aided diagnosis because its screening workflow is standardized and large color fundus datasets are available. Early systems emphasized lesion-specific analysis of microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, and neovascularization for interpretable grading, as illustrated by classic microaneurysm detectors and red-lesion pipelines ref [101], ref [102]. With the growth of curated screening benchmarks, algorithm development shifted toward image-level severity classification and referable-DR detection using public datasets such as Messidor and EyePACS, enabling direct comparison between handcrafted and deep learning methods ref [60], ref [103].

Deep convolutional models markedly improved performance by learning hierarchical retinal features directly from pixels. Landmark studies demonstrated that end-to-end networks could achieve high sensitivity and specificity for referable DR from fundus photographs, motivating regulatory and clinical translation ref [1], ref [2]. Subsequent work also showed that deep models can predict center-involved diabetic macular edema (DME) risk from fundus images alone, despite DME being more directly characterized on optical coherence tomography (OCT), suggesting that subtle vascular and exudative cues can be exploited computationally ref [104].

For DME specifically, CAD systems increasingly integrate OCT for fluid, retinal thickness, and layer-disruption assessment. Deep architectures for retinal fluid segmentation and diabetic OCT classification support the transition from 2D color screening to multimodal disease management ref [105], ref [106]. Recent validation studies further indicate that autonomous AI can be embedded in point-of-care DR screening pathways, although performance remains sensitive to image quality, population shift, and the clinically important distinction between detection, grading, and treatment referral ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Disease-Specific Computer-Aided Diagnostic Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Glaucoma and optic neuropathy
subsections.content:
Glaucoma-oriented CAD systems are shaped by the disease’s structural biomarkers, particularly optic disc cupping, neuroretinal rim thinning, retinal nerve fiber layer loss, and peripapillary changes visible in color fundus photographs and OCT. Early work therefore emphasized automated optic disc/cup localization and cup-to-disc ratio estimation from fundus images, often as a proxy for screening risk, while later systems incorporated end-to-end deep learning for referral decisions. Representative fundus-based studies include convolutional and ranking-based screening models evaluated on large clinical datasets such as DeepCDR and related disc/cup segmentation pipelines, which improved glaucoma discrimination by explicitly modeling the optic nerve head anatomy ref [107], ref [108], ref [109].

A major trend has been the shift from handcrafted morphometrics to multimodal and three-dimensional learning from OCT, where glaucomatous damage can be quantified at the level of RNFL, ganglion cell complex, and lamina-associated structures. Deep models trained on raw OCT cubes or circumpapillary scans have shown that machine learning can approach specialist-level detection and severity stratification, while segmentation frameworks for OCT support biomarker extraction and longitudinal analysis ref [110], ref [111], ref [112]. These approaches are especially relevant for preperimetric glaucoma and for distinguishing true progression from anatomical variability.

For optic neuropathy more broadly, CAD methods must address overlapping phenotypes across glaucoma, ischemic and compressive neuropathies, and myopic optic disc deformation. This has motivated domain-shift-aware learning, multimodal fusion, and uncertainty-aware referral systems rather than single-threshold screening tools. Public benchmarks such as REFUGE and large-scale development studies have accelerated standardized evaluation of optic disc segmentation and glaucoma classification, but clinically robust deployment still depends on external validation across devices, populations, and disease subtypes ref [113], ref [114], ref [115].

subsections.section_title: Disease-Specific Computer-Aided Diagnostic Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Age-related macular degeneration and retinal degeneration
subsections.content:
Computer-aided diagnosis for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is shaped by multimodal biomarkers spanning color fundus photography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus autofluorescence, and angiography. Early systems emphasized lesion detection and grading from fundus images, including drusen quantification and discrimination of early versus late AMD, while later deep learning models expanded to automated referral and disease severity estimation. The AREDS group established clinically meaningful severity scales for AMD progression, which have strongly influenced algorithmic target definitions and evaluation protocols ref [116]. On color fundus photographs, deep convolutional systems have achieved expert-level performance for referable AMD and related retinal diseases in large screening settings ref [1].

OCT-driven CAD has become central because it directly captures subretinal fluid, intraretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachments, and drusen morphology. Deep architectures have been used to classify urgent macular disease and distinguish neovascular AMD from other causes of macular pathology on OCT volumes and B-scans ref [10], ref [117]. Beyond diagnosis, segmentation-oriented methods support quantitative biomarker extraction; for example, automated segmentation of geographic atrophy and drusen in spectral-domain OCT enables longitudinal assessment of retinal pigment epithelium and outer retinal loss ref [118]. Such approaches are increasingly linked to prognosis, treatment monitoring, and anti-VEGF response assessment rather than simple cross-sectional categorization.

Retinal degeneration more broadly includes inherited retinal diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and Stargardt disease, where CAD tasks often shift from binary diagnosis to structure-function phenotyping and progression modeling. Deep learning on fundus autofluorescence has been used to delineate atrophic or hyperautofluorescent regions relevant to inherited degeneration and AMD-related geographic atrophy ref [119]. For AMD prognosis, deep models trained on OCT and clinical variables have shown value in predicting conversion to exudative disease and future visual outcomes ref [24], ref [120]. More recently, self-supervised and foundation-style retinal representations have improved transfer across diverse posterior segment tasks, suggesting a path toward unified models spanning AMD, geographic atrophy, and inherited retinal degeneration despite limited labels in rare diseases ref [121].

subsections.section_title: Disease-Specific Computer-Aided Diagnostic Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Cataract and anterior segment disorders
subsections.content:
Computer-aided diagnosis for cataract and anterior segment disorders differs from fundus-centered pipelines because pathology is expressed in slit-lamp photographs, retroillumination images, anterior-segment OCT, specular microscopy, and corneal topography rather than retinal structure. Early work on cataract emphasized automatic grading from slit-lamp or fundus photographs, including detection of nuclear and cortical opacity severity and referral-level screening in community settings ref [122], ref [123]. More recent deep learning studies have pursued clinically deployable systems that jointly identify cataract and urgent coexisting conditions, reflecting the practical need to triage low-quality images, media opacity, and surgically significant lens changes ref [124], ref [125].

Within corneal disease, keratoconus has been a major target because diagnosis relies on subtle geometric and biomechanical abnormalities that are well suited to machine learning on topography/tomography. Large comparative studies have shown high accuracy for detecting clinical and subclinical keratoconus using Scheimpflug-derived features and conventional classifiers ref [126], while deep neural approaches have extended this paradigm to raw corneal maps and multimodal indices for screening and progression risk stratification ref [127]. In infectious keratitis and other surface disorders, image-based deep learning has also been explored for rapid triage from slit-lamp photographs, potentially supporting referral in resource-limited settings ref [128].

Anterior segment CAD has additionally expanded to surgical planning and tissue-level assessment. For example, automated endothelial cell analysis from specular microscopy has been addressed with convolutional networks to estimate cell density and morphology more robustly than traditional segmentation pipelines ref [129]. Other studies have used anterior-segment OCT and slit-lamp images to classify angle closure or lens status, linking CAD not only to disease recognition but also to perioperative risk assessment and treatment selection ref [130]. Overall, the field is characterized by modality heterogeneity, smaller datasets than in retinal imaging, and a strong requirement for image-quality control and clinically interpretable outputs.

subsections.section_title: Disease-Specific Computer-Aided Diagnostic Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Retinal vascular and miscellaneous ocular diseases
subsections.content:
Beyond diabetic retinopathy, computer-aided diagnosis for retinal vascular disorders has focused on lesions whose appearance is strongly geometry- and perfusion-dependent, including vessel caliber changes, tortuosity, nonperfusion, and aneurysmal dilatation. Early automated systems emphasized vessel extraction as a prerequisite for quantifying arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nicking in hypertensive and occlusive disease; representative methods include the two-dimensional matched-filter approach of Chaudhuri et al. and the multiscale line-operator segmentation of Nguyen et al. [1,2]. Public benchmarks such as DRIVE and STARE enabled more reproducible evaluation of these pipelines and accelerated the transition from handcrafted feature engineering to learning-based vascular analysis [3,4].

For retinal vein occlusion and ischemic retinopathies, recent models integrate color fundus photography with fluorescein angiography or OCT/OCTA to capture both structural and perfusion abnormalities. Deep systems have been developed for wide-field angiographic detection of nonperfusion and leakage, as illustrated by automated ultra-widefield fluorescein angiography analysis for diabetic retinopathy by Ehlers et al., a paradigm readily transferable to vein occlusion and vasculitis assessment [5]. On OCTA, quantitative descriptors of vessel density and foveal avascular zone disruption have been shown to support automated discrimination of retinal vascular pathology, with review evidence summarized by de Carlo et al. and Spaide et al. [6,7].

A miscellaneous but clinically important group includes retinopathy of prematurity, inherited telangiectatic disorders, and inflammatory or infectious retinopathies. In retinopathy of prematurity, image analysis has centered on plus disease, where vascular tortuosity and dilation are dominant biomarkers; the i-ROP system reported by Brown et al. demonstrated that deep learning can achieve expert-level severity assessment from retinal images [8]. More broadly, reviews of AI in ophthalmic imaging highlight that rare vascular diseases remain constrained by limited labeled datasets, domain shift across cameras, and the need for lesion-specific explainability, making weak supervision, multimodal fusion, and calibrated uncertainty especially relevant for deployment [9,10].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Interpretability
subsections.subsection_title: Evaluation metrics and benchmarking strategies
subsections.content:
Evaluation of ocular computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems depends strongly on task formulation. For screening-oriented classifiers, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and sometimes area under the precision-recall curve are standard, but they should be reported at clinically meaningful operating points because disease prevalence and referral costs are highly asymmetric. This principle is evident in diabetic retinopathy studies that emphasized high-sensitivity triage performance rather than AUROC alone, including large development and validation efforts on retinal fundus photographs ref [1], ref [28]. For glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration, class imbalance and label uncertainty further motivate confidence intervals, calibration assessment, and stratified reporting across disease severity rather than single aggregate scores ref [140], ref [10].

Benchmarking strategies should therefore go beyond random internal test splits. Public datasets such as Messidor have enabled some comparability, but performance estimates remain sensitive to image quality filters, per-image versus per-eye aggregation, and hidden correlations between training and test sets ref [141]. Rigorous studies increasingly use patient-level separation, predefined protocols, and external datasets acquired with different cameras or institutions, as illustrated in OCT- and fundus-based deep learning evaluations ref [142], ref [9]. For segmentation tasks, overlap-based measures such as Dice or Jaccard are useful but insufficient alone; boundary error and structure-specific metrics may better reflect whether optic disc, cup, or lesion delineations support downstream clinical decisions ref [143].

A robust benchmarking framework should also compare models against clinicians and established risk thresholds. Reader-study style comparisons and prospective or temporally separated test sets help determine whether measured gains are practically meaningful, as shown in autonomous diabetic retinopathy assessment and broader guidelines for prediction-model validation ref [28], ref [144], ref [145]. Overall, ocular CAD benchmarks are most informative when they combine discrimination, calibration, decision-threshold analysis, and external reproducibility.

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Interpretability
subsections.subsection_title: External validation and generalization
subsections.content:
External validation is essential in ocular CAD because apparent in-distribution performance often degrades when algorithms are tested across different cameras, acquisition protocols, disease prevalence, ethnic composition, and referral settings. This issue was highlighted early in diabetic retinopathy screening, where high internal accuracy did not automatically imply portability across health systems, motivating multi-site evaluation and prospective assessment ref [1], ref [146]. More recent reviews of ophthalmic AI have similarly emphasized that spectrum bias, image-quality differences, and label variability can make single-center retrospective results overly optimistic ref [147].

Evidence from multi-national validation studies shows both the promise and fragility of generalization. Deep-learning systems for diabetic retinopathy achieved strong performance across datasets collected in Thailand, India, and other regions, yet performance still depended on gradability standards and workflow integration ref [146], ref [28]. In age-related macular degeneration and retinal OCT analysis, externally tested systems have demonstrated clinically relevant discrimination, but domain shifts in scanner vendor, segmentation conventions, and case mix remain persistent sources of error ref [10], ref [148]. Similar concerns arise in glaucoma, where models trained on fundus photographs or OCT may exploit site-specific correlates rather than disease biology unless carefully stress-tested across institutions ref [149].

Accordingly, robust generalization assessment should move beyond random train-test splits toward geographic, temporal, and device-level holdout designs, with prespecified subgroup analyses and calibration reporting. Public benchmark initiatives such as REFUGE and large real-world datasets such as ODIR have helped standardize cross-dataset comparison, although true clinical validation still requires prospective, workflow-aware studies and transparent reporting of failure modes ref [113], ref [150], ref [151].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Interpretability
subsections.subsection_title: Explainability and clinician trust
subsections.content:
Explainability is central to clinician trust in ocular CAD because image-based predictions must be reconciled with recognizable anatomical cues such as hemorrhages, exudates, optic disc changes, or fluid compartments on OCT. In ophthalmology, most deployed explanation interfaces rely on post hoc visual attribution, especially class activation mapping and its variants, to highlight retinal regions supporting a decision. These methods have been widely used in diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and OCT-based referral systems, but their role is primarily supportive: heatmaps can improve face validity and error analysis, yet they do not by themselves guarantee that a model has learned clinically appropriate features ref [152], ref [1], ref [10].

A recurring concern is that saliency maps may appear plausible even when models exploit confounders or preprocessing artifacts. More general work on explainability has shown that many attribution methods are unstable or weakly tied to model reasoning, cautioning against equating visual explanation with causal transparency ref [153], ref [154]. In ophthalmic AI, this has motivated stronger forms of interpretability, including lesion-level supervision, segmentation-assisted pipelines, and concept- or feature-based explanations that align predictions with human-interpretable biomarkers. Examples include attention or localization frameworks for diabetic retinopathy lesions and OCT systems that expose tissue or fluid compartments associated with disease activity ref [155], ref [3], ref [156].

Clinician trust also depends on whether explanations are calibrated to workflow. Human-factors studies suggest that trust is better supported when systems communicate uncertainty, failure modes, and clinically meaningful evidence rather than only binary outputs ref [157]. More broadly, rigorous reporting and transparent model documentation are increasingly viewed as prerequisites for trustworthy medical AI, complementing technical explainability with governance, validation, and accountability practices ref [158].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Interpretability
subsections.subsection_title: Human-AI collaboration and reader studies
subsections.content:
Human–AI collaboration studies in ocular CAD increasingly move beyond stand-alone accuracy to ask whether AI assistance improves clinician performance, efficiency, and consistency. In diabetic retinopathy screening, randomized and multi-reader evaluations have shown that deep learning systems can reach specialist-level performance and, when embedded into grading workflows, can support triage or second-reader paradigms rather than fully autonomous replacement ref [1], ref [28]. Similar reader-study designs are emerging in glaucoma and OCT-based retinal disease assessment, where the relevant endpoints include changes in sensitivity for referable disease, inter-grader agreement, and time to decision under AI assistance ref [10], ref [159].

A key lesson from these studies is that assistance effects are heterogeneous: AI can improve non-expert readers most, but may also induce over-reliance, automation bias, or reduced vigilance when model outputs are presented without calibrated uncertainty or adequate explanation. This concern is highlighted by broader evidence that clinicians can be misled by incorrect AI suggestions and that the benefit of assistance depends strongly on interface design and the user's baseline expertise ref [160], ref [161]. For ocular applications, this implies that reader studies should report not only mean performance gains but also error redistribution, subgroup effects, and how clinicians respond to discordant AI recommendations.

Methodologically, rigorous reader studies in ophthalmology should therefore use representative case mixes, counterbalanced crossover or multi-reader multi-case designs, and clinically meaningful outcomes such as referral accuracy, downstream workload, and adjudicated patient-level safety. Prospective deployment studies further suggest that workflow integration, image quality control, and referral pathways are as important as algorithmic discrimination for real-world benefit ref [162], ref [163]. Future human–AI evaluations should test collaborative protocols explicitly—such as arbitration after disagreement, uncertainty-triggered referral, or expert review of AI-flagged edge cases—to determine when combined systems outperform either humans or models alone ref [164], ref [165].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Ethical Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Data scarcity, imbalance, and annotation noise
subsections.content:
Data limitations remain a central bottleneck for ocular CAD. Public ophthalmic datasets are typically modest in size, concentrated in a few diseases, and acquired under narrow imaging protocols, as illustrated by benchmark collections such as Messidor for diabetic retinopathy, DRIVE and STARE for vessel analysis, and REFUGE for optic disc/cup and glaucoma assessment [1,2,3,4]. Such datasets have accelerated method development, but they also expose a persistent gap between research benchmarks and the diversity encountered in clinical deployment, where prevalence is low for many target conditions and image quality, devices, and populations vary substantially.

Class imbalance is especially acute in screening settings, where referable disease, rare retinal findings, and longitudinal progression cases are heavily underrepresented. This can inflate apparent performance on aggregate metrics while degrading sensitivity for minority classes or subtle lesions. Prior studies on diabetic retinopathy grading and lesion detection have highlighted both the dependence of deep models on large-scale curation and the vulnerability of learning under skewed label distributions [5,6]. In practice, mitigation strategies include cost-sensitive losses, hard-example mining, synthetic augmentation, and more informative evaluation with per-class sensitivity, calibration, and prevalence-aware metrics rather than accuracy alone.

Annotation noise further complicates supervision because many ocular labels are subjective, hierarchical, and based on imperfect human grading. Large tele-ophthalmology studies have shown substantial gains from adjudication and multi-grader consensus, underscoring that disagreement is not merely nuisance but a signal of label uncertainty [7,8]. Similar concerns arise in glaucoma, where structural labels are influenced by disc morphology and grader expertise, motivating robust learning with soft labels, uncertainty modeling, and quality-aware training [4,9]. Future progress will depend on richer multicenter datasets, standardized protocols, and semi-supervised or self-supervised representation learning that reduces dependence on exhaustive manual annotation [10].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Ethical Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Robustness, fairness, and bias in ocular AI
subsections.content:
Robustness remains a central barrier to trustworthy ocular AI because model performance can deteriorate under distribution shift across cameras, acquisition protocols, disease prevalence, and clinical sites. Large-scale retinal benchmarks have demonstrated strong average accuracy for diabetic retinopathy screening, yet external validation studies also show that performance is sensitive to image quality, gradability, and population differences, underscoring the gap between retrospective development and real-world deployment ref [1], ref [9], ref [28]. More broadly, recommendations for medical imaging AI emphasize stress-testing under dataset shift, calibration analysis, and uncertainty-aware evaluation rather than reporting only internal test-set AUROC ref [173].

Fairness and bias are equally important in ophthalmology because fundus and OCT datasets often underrepresent particular racial, ethnic, age, or socioeconomic groups. A major concern is that ostensibly disease-focused models can encode demographic information from retinal images, creating pathways for subgroup-dependent errors and potentially amplifying inequities in access or triage ref [174]. Evidence that medical imaging models may exploit spurious shortcuts rather than robust pathology signals further motivates causal evaluation and cross-domain auditing in ocular settings ref [175]. In parallel, subgroup assessment should move beyond aggregate metrics to stratified sensitivity, calibration, and error analysis across protected attributes and imaging conditions ref [173], ref [176].

Future work should prioritize multicenter prospective validation, fairness-aware dataset curation, and methods that improve both robustness and equity, such as domain generalization, distributionally robust optimization, and uncertainty-based deferral. Regulatory guidance for AI/ML-enabled medical devices increasingly stresses transparency, real-world monitoring, and management of performance drift, which is highly relevant for continuously updated ocular systems ref [177]. Emerging reporting frameworks for clinical AI and prediction models can support this transition by standardizing documentation of participant demographics, data provenance, and subgroup performance ref [151], ref [178].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Ethical Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Privacy, regulation, and translational barriers
subsections.content:
Privacy remains a central obstacle to ocular CAD deployment because retinal photographs and OCT volumes are inherently identifiable biomarkers, and model inversion or membership-inference attacks can leak sensitive patient information even when only model outputs are exposed ref [179], ref [180]. Regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR and HIPAA therefore constrain data sharing, cross-border aggregation, and secondary use, motivating privacy-preserving development pipelines and careful governance for ophthalmic datasets ref [181]. Yet stronger privacy mechanisms may reduce utility, creating a practical tension between confidentiality and clinically acceptable diagnostic performance.

Translation is also limited by regulation of adaptive AI systems. The CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI extensions emphasize transparent reporting of intended use, human-AI interaction, input handling, and error analysis in clinical trials ref [182], ref [183]. More broadly, Good Machine Learning Practice for medical devices and the FDA’s proposed framework for AI/ML-based software as a medical device highlight the need for lifecycle monitoring, change control, and real-world performance surveillance rather than one-time validation ref [184], ref [185]. For ophthalmology, this is especially important because image acquisition protocols, devices, and referral thresholds vary substantially across screening programs and care settings.

A further translational barrier is the gap between retrospective benchmark accuracy and prospective clinical benefit. Early autonomous diabetic retinopathy systems demonstrated feasibility in real-world primary care, but also underscored the importance of workflow integration, image quality control, referral logistics, reimbursement, and clinician accountability ref [28], ref [163]. Recent reviews of AI regulation in medicine likewise argue that trustworthiness depends not only on technical performance but also on documentation, post-market auditing, and local validation before deployment ref [186]. Future ocular CAD systems should therefore be designed with privacy engineering, regulatory science, and implementation pathways in mind from the outset.

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Ethical Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Federated learning, foundation models, and multimodal intelligence
subsections.content:
Federated learning (FL) is a promising response to the fragmented and privacy-sensitive nature of ophthalmic data, allowing institutions to train shared models without centralizing images or records. The general FL paradigm established by FedAvg has been adapted widely in medical imaging, where cross-site heterogeneity, label scarcity, and communication constraints remain central obstacles ref [187], ref [188]. In eye care, these issues are amplified by device-specific retinal appearance, differing screening workflows, and uneven disease prevalence, so future FL systems must move beyond simple parameter averaging toward personalization, domain generalization, and secure auditing.

Recent studies suggest that foundation-model style pretraining can mitigate annotation bottlenecks by transferring broad visual representations into ophthalmic tasks. In medical imaging, scalable self-supervised approaches such as masked autoencoding and generalist segmentation models have shown that large pretrained encoders can improve sample efficiency and robustness ref [100], ref [189]. Parallel progress in ophthalmology has demonstrated that self-supervised learning on retinal images can yield transferable features for downstream diagnosis and prognosis ref [190], while multimodal retinal foundation models further point to a route for unifying color fundus photography, OCT, and associated text or metadata within a single representation space ref [191].

A key future direction is multimodal intelligence that combines imaging with longitudinal electronic health records, genomics, visual function, and treatment history to support risk prediction and individualized management. Large multimodal models in biomedicine and ophthalmology indicate that cross-modal alignment can improve both predictive performance and clinical usability ref [192], ref [193]. However, deploying such systems safely will require careful evaluation of calibration, subgroup fairness, and failure modes, particularly when combining FL with large pretrained models whose data provenance and adaptation behavior may be opaque ref [194].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Ethical Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Toward personalized and proactive ophthalmic care
subsections.content:
A key future direction for ocular CAD is to move beyond one-shot detection toward personalized, longitudinal, and preventive care. Large-scale retinal imaging studies have shown that ocular photographs encode systemic and cardiovascular risk factors, suggesting that eye-based AI can support broader risk stratification and earlier intervention rather than only lesion recognition ref [40], ref [1]. Likewise, multimodal deep learning on optical coherence tomography (OCT) and electronic health record data has demonstrated the feasibility of predicting future referral needs in retinal disease clinics, a practical step toward anticipatory service planning and individualized follow-up ref [195].

Personalization will require models that integrate baseline phenotype, disease subtype, treatment history, and temporal imaging trajectories. In age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, deep learning systems have already been used to predict conversion or progression from longitudinal OCT or fundus data, indicating that prognosis-oriented modeling is achievable when repeated observations are available ref [24], ref [196], ref [197]. More broadly, clinically meaningful deployment will depend on combining image biomarkers with patient-specific covariates and uncertainty estimates so that recommendations can be adapted to heterogeneous risks, treatment burdens, and resource constraints ref [10], ref [198].

Realizing proactive ophthalmic care also raises implementation challenges: longitudinal labels are sparse, follow-up is irregular, and outcome definitions vary across institutions. Foundation models and self-supervised learning may help exploit large unlabeled archives, but prospective validation, continual monitoring, and workflow-aware decision support remain essential to ensure that personalized predictions improve outcomes rather than simply automate triage ref [199], ref [200].
